To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Holocaust has left its imprint on the German national psyche.

(1) the Holocaust was an extreme event, which was traumatic for all those involved; (2) the trauma was not only a personal experience but also a social one, which was transmitted from one generation to another; (3) the trauma was transmitted through the family narratives; (4) the family narratives were organized by dissociative processes and by the affective processes of shame and guilt; and (5) these narratives are transmitted unconsciously, and they are not accessible through conscious memory.
(a) the Holocaust is not a historical event, but rather a traumatic experience that has been inherited by the descendants of the perpetrators and the victims.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of memory and the past in the construction of identity.
the relationship between inherited traumatic memory, narrative memory and moral response.
the question of how the traumatic past can be understood in the present, and how it might be possible to create a new future.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
'the limits of understanding are not the limits of experience' (p. 106).
the Holocaust is a traumatic historical event that is not only a part of history but also an event that is transmitted in family narrative.
the Holocaust was a unique and unparalleled historical event.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Holocaust is an example for the fact that the limits of understanding are not only the result of the limits of the human mind.
the Holocaust is a historical event that can never be completely understood by the descendants of the perpetrators or victims.
the article is about how we understand and remember our past, and how that past shapes the present.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the limits of understanding and the limits of our moral imagination are not fixed but are always in the process of becoming.
we must be aware of the limits of our understanding of others, and of the limits of their understanding of us.
the limits of understanding are not only a problem of history, but also a problem of the human psyche.
